title: Federal Hemp Ban 2026: Trump Backed CBD, Congress Banned It ft. Paige Figi
description:
On November 12, 2026, a provision buried in the spending bill that ended the longest government shutdown in U.S. history takes effect and rewrites the federal definition of hemp, capping finished hemp products at 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. Paige Figi, founder of Coalition for Access Now and mother of Charlotte Figi, joins The Dime to explain what the federal hemp ban does to therapeutic CBD, who loses access, and why the licensed cannabis industry is misreading it as a win.

The 2018 Farm Bill descheduled hemp but never finished the job. The original bills paired descheduling with FDA regulation, and only the first half passed. Roughly four thousand hemp CBD companies built businesses in the eight unregulated years that followed, and almost none of them paid to write the rulebook that would have protected them. Two members of Congress wrote the ban into a must-pass appropriations bill with no conference and no regular order. According to the U.S. Hemp Roundtable, more than 90 percent of non-intoxicating CBD products currently on shelves exceed the new per-container limit. Meanwhile the Trump administration opened Medicare to hemp-derived CBD in April 2026, up to $500 per year for eligible patients, built around the full-spectrum products the November cap would make illegal.

In this conversation:

● What changes on November 12, 2026, and why 0.4 milligrams per container is the number that matters

● Why CBD isolate is not a clinical substitute for full-spectrum therapeutic hemp

● Dispensary deserts, age gating, and what access looks like for pediatric patients

● The Medicare CBD pilot, Dr. Oz, and the contradiction inside federal policy

● Why two members of Congress were enough, and what that precedent means for marijuana

● The 60-email threshold Paige Figi says moves an issue to the top of a senator's desk

Paige Figi is the founder of Coalition for Access Now at Coalition For Access Now – Home . Her daughter Charlotte Figi's response to full-spectrum CBD is widely credited with changing American public opinion on cannabis as medicine.

Subscribe for operator-level cannabis and hemp conversations every week.

title: The Truth About Using AI To Build Software ft. Chris Guthrie
description:
What actually happens when you use AI to build your own software over a weekend? Vibe coding makes building tools feel as simple as a few hours, but an MVP that works on Saturday is not an enterprise grade tool that survives your team on a Friday night. Chris Guthrie of 365 Cannabis has spent six years deploying Microsoft Business Central for cannabis companies, and he has watched this exact decision quietly wreck operators who thought they were saving money. This conversation is for cannabis founders, CEOs, COOs, and CFOs weighing whether to build internal software with AI or invest in a real ERP foundation.

The pitch sounds good. AI makes software easy, capital is scarce, and building your own cannabis CRM or ERP feels like leverage. The problem is what sits underneath it. Most cannabis software is descriptive data, a record of what already happened, and no amount of vibe coding turns a record of the past into the predictive tools an operator needs to forecast yield, standard cost, and labor. Build it on a shaky foundation and you inherit tech debt you cannot see, right as M&A and possible FDA oversight force the industry to show clean books.

In this conversation on cannabis technology and operational discipline:

● Why vibe coding a cannabis ERP builds hidden tech debt and AI drift

● Descriptive data versus predictive data, and why seed to sale falls short

● What Microsoft Business Central and hardened ERP infrastructure actually buy you

● The real cost math of a weekend build, in CFO hours, not software licenses

● Clean books, standard cost, and readiness for cannabis M&A and FDA rules

title: Cannabis Rescheduling: The DEA Hearing That Could Pick Winners ft. Hirsh Jain
description:
Did Trump reschedule cannabis? Not the way the headlines told you. In this episode of The Dime, Hirsh Jain of Ananda Strategy breaks down what the April Schedule III order actually did, why medical and adult-use cannabis were split into two separate tracks, and what the June 29 DEA hearing means for cannabis operators, MSOs, and investors tracking interstate commerce.

Here is the tension nobody is naming. Medical cannabis moved to Schedule III. Adult use stayed Schedule I. The DEA opened a registration portal full of self-incriminating questions, and state regulators are quietly positioning to block interstate commerce and protect their own markets. Hirsh explains how cannabis rescheduling is already sorting the industry into winners and losers, and why the states that designed their license structures years ago may decide who survives the next phase of federal cannabis policy.

What we get into:

● What Schedule III actually unlocks for cannabis businesses, and what it doesn't

● The DEA registration portal, the deadline, and the real risk of applying

● Three state models emerging: Oklahoma, California, and Washington

● Interstate commerce, the dormant commerce clause, and the FDA approval hurdle

● Why Georgia, Texas, and Arkansas are the red-state cannabis markets to watch

This is an operator-to-operator breakdown of cannabis rescheduling, the DEA hearing, federal policy, and the strategic decisions facing every license holder right now.

The Dime covers cannabis industry strategy, regulatory analysis, and operator interviews with the people actually building this market. Subscribe, follow, and send this to someone trying to make sense of rescheduling.

title: Taking a 6,000-Compound Cannabis Plant Through the FDA ft. Joel Stanley and Dr. Marcel Bonn-Miller
description:
Joel Stanley co-founded Charlotte's Web and spent a decade building the most standardized botanical cannabis operation in the world. Then he left to start Ajna Biosciences. The FDA quietly opened a botanical drug development pathway in 2016 that most of the cannabis industry, and most investors, have never heard of. Dr. Marcel Bonn-Miller has spent 23 years in cannabinoid research, built the world's largest cannabis research registry alongside Johns Hopkins, and now serves as the scientific backbone behind the most advanced botanical drug program in the space.

Their lead drug, AJA-001, is a full-spectrum Charlotte's Web derived formula targeting irritability and aggression in autism spectrum disorder. It contains over 6,000 identified compounds. It is backed by British American Tobacco through a partnership called Defloria. And it is about to enter phase two clinical trials.

This is not a supplement story. This is FDA drug development, the same approval groups, the same clinical rigor, the same regulatory pathway as Pfizer or Lilly, applied to a plant that has been used as medicine for centuries.

What most investors get wrong is the risk profile. Because these cannabinoid molecules have decades of real world human use data, botanical drugs can advance directly to phase two. New synthetic chemical entities cannot. The front end is harder because you are characterizing thousands of compounds instead of one. The back end is substantially de-risked because the safety data already exists. That is a different equation than conventional pharma, and almost no one in the investment community understands it yet.

Inside this episode:

●Why the green rush buried the cannabis medical thesis and what that cost the industry

●How Charlotte's Web standardized a 6,000-compound plant to pharmaceutical specifications

●The FDA botanical drug pathway that has existed since 2016 and why most investors have never heard of it

●AJA-001, the autism pipeline, and the British American Tobacco partnership behind it

●Novel cannabinoid compounds being discovered and categorized that do not exist in any known scientific database

●Why full-spectrum botanical medicine requires lower doses for equivalent efficacy compared to synthetic isolates

●How AI and supercomputing are accelerating compound identification in botanical drug discovery

●Why organic botanical medicine will be a real choice at the pharmacy counter sooner than most people expect

title: Ed Rosenthal & Greg Baughman: The Cannabis Industry Is Growing Flower Wrong
description:
Ed Rosenthal wrote the books that trained a generation of cannabis growers. Now he's pointing at the part of the operation most of them still haven't fixed: what happens after the plant comes down.

The cannabis consumer walking into a dispensary today has no reliable way to know if what they're buying is fresh. Harvest dates are on the label but not the storage conditions, not the dry room time, not how long it sat in the back before it hit the shelf. Brands take the blame for a consistency problem built into the supply chain itself, and most operators don't know where the loss is actually happening.

In indoor Canadian operations producing flower at 55 cents a gram, 60% of that cost is sitting in post-harvest. Not cultivation. The dry room, the trim, the handling, the energy, the labor

This week we sit down with Ed Rosenthal and Greg Baughman to discuss:

● How Canada already solved this
● Why most are still cultivating wrong
● Freeze drying vs. traditional drying

description:
$160 million spent on Florida. Couldn't raise $20K for two days with Congress. The cannabis industry has no idea how power works in Washington — and it's why nothing changes.

Gretchen Gailey spent 20+ years on Capitol Hill. She's seen every mistake: fly-ins that get forgotten, money thrown at politicians who don't care, an industry built by radicals now terrified of playing offense. Her solution? Stab them in the back, push them down the stairs, and make sure everyone knows cannabis did it.

This episode breaks down why cannabis is popular but not important, how she got a small operator her license in 48 hours by putting a camera in Cory Booker's face, and why the industry keeps lobbying for carve-outs when there's no federal foundation.

If you're wondering why DC ignores cannabis — this is the answer.

This week we sit down with Gretchen Gailey:

● Stab them in the back politics

● Curtains before basement problem

● Project Champion playbook

title: MSOS Bear Playbook Exposed Everything I Learned in 15 Years Trading Cannabis Stocks | Dan McDermitt
description:
Dan McDermitt has been trading cannabis stocks for 15 years — before Colorado legalized, before MSOS existed, before most traders knew the sector was tradeable. He's seen every pump, every dump, and every slow bleed back to where it started.

In this episode, Dan breaks down the bear playbook that keeps working: headline drops, algos spike MSOS, it halts, tops out at resistance, and slow bleeds for days. Rinse and repeat. He explains why this pattern persists, why time favors the bears as long as DC moves slowly, and why retail keeps getting caught in the same trap.

He also challenges the belief most investors cling to — that they're "early." His take: if you've been through multiple pump-and-dump cycles, you're not early anymore. You're just still here. And there's a ceiling on every rally created by bag holders underwater who just want to break even.

This conversation covers how to think about cannabis stocks as a trader, not a believer — and why Dan already knows he'll sell early on the next catalyst.

This week we sit down with Dan McDermitt:

•The "I'm early" delusion

title: Premium vs Scale in Cannabis: Why Rubicon Chose Quality Over Expansion ft. Margaret Brodie
description:
Most cannabis companies chased scale. Rubicon chased quality.

As legalization expanded, the dominant strategy across the cannabis industry was simple: grow bigger, expand into more markets, and compete on price. But Rubicon Organics took a different path. Instead of prioritizing expansion, they focused on building a premium cannabis brand centered on consistent flower quality and consumer trust.

In this episode of The Dime, Margaret Brodie, CEO of Rubicon Organics, explains why premium cannabis is harder than most companies realize, why many cannabis brands fail to deliver on quality, and how consumer trust is still one of the most valuable assets in the industry.

The conversation also explores how operators think about resource allocation, internal operational audits, and why Europe could become one of the most important future markets for premium cannabis brands.

If cannabis ultimately becomes a commodity market, can premium brands survive? Or will scale always win?

In this episode we discuss:

• Why most cannabis brands struggle to maintain consistent quality

• The difference between premium cannabis and premium branding

• Why consumers give cannabis brands only one chance

• How Rubicon evaluates operations, resources, and priorities

• The role of trust in building long-term cannabis brands

• Why Europe could become a major opportunity for premium cannabis companies

About Margaret Brodie

Margaret Brodie is the CEO of Rubicon Organics, an industry leader in organic certified and premium cannabis brands. The company trades on the TSXV under ROMJ and OTCQX under ROMJF. Under her leadership, Rubicon has focused on disciplined growth, premium flower quality, and building trusted cannabis brands.

Setbacks early on can reshape everything.
They can alter your future strategy, shift your appetite for risk, and — if you’re patient — quietly set you up for success while others chase growth at any cost.

As with any company, “figuring it out” is part of the job. And sometimes, that figuring it out happens faster than you’d ever hope.

The challenges you face early in your cannabis journey become the lens you see the world through — for better or worse. Those lessons, combined with the financial discipline from previous chapters of life, shape your decision-making, your culture, and your tolerance for this chaotic industry.

And as cannabis braces for consolidation and a $6B debt wall, that slow, methodical approach might prove to be the ultimate advantage.

This week we sit down with Jared Maloof, CEO of Standard Wellness, to discuss:
• How early mistakes built long-term discipline
• Why focused, prudent capital deployment became Standard’s superpower
• The playbook across Utah, Ohio, and beyond
• Conversations with Carl Icahn

title: Chris Ball on The Real Story Behind Ball Family Farms ft. Chris Ball
description:
Building something that lasts takes more than money — it takes self-belief, grit, and the willingness to keep pushing forward when easier options present themselves.

Putting your name on it only adds to the weight — and the responsibility — to make it work.

As with anything worth doing, there are difficult moments along the journey that demand a leap of faith.

If you want to be different, you have to be willing to swim against the current — to stand out long enough for customers to find their fit.

Daniel LaRusso was that choice for Chris Ball. A nod to his movie-buff personality, the name sent a subtle but direct message to his audience about grit, discipline, and staying true to the craft.

These decisions are easy to reflect on now, but the journey was anything but simple.

This week we sit down with Chris Ball, Founder of Ball Family Farms, to discuss:

• The journey from origin to now — and the critical decisions that shaped it
• How he’s constantly tinkering forward to stay ahead
• The Rare Breed mentorship program and its impact on the next generation of growers

Summary

In this episode, Chris Ball, CEO of Ball Family Farms, shares his journey from the legacy cannabis market to establishing a successful legal cannabis business. He discusses the importance of family in building his brand, the challenges of navigating the cannabis industry, and the significance of quality over quantity in product development. Chris also highlights the role of mentorship through his Rare Breed program, which aims to nurture new talent in the cannabis space. He emphasizes the need for innovation while maintaining a connection to the community and culture of cannabis. The conversation concludes with insights into the realities of being a CEO in the cannabis industry and the importance of resilience and adaptability.

title: Largest Cannabis & Cancer Study Ever: 10,000 Papers, Top 5% Worldwide ft. Ryan Castle
description:
If you were given some of the worst news in the world, wouldn’t you expect your doctors to use every tool available?

What if one of those tools could save millions of lives—and the science is already here?

The world’s largest medical cannabis and cancer study—10,000 papers, ranked in the top 5% globally—shows overwhelming evidence that cannabis has medical benefits. If fully embraced, its impact on patients and medicine could be transformative. As science continues to unfold, sometimes it takes skeptics to dive deep and uncover what’s truly there, even when powerful interests push back.

This week we sit down with Ryan Castle, Research Director at Whole Health Oncology Institute, to discuss:

• Medical cannabis: efficacy, placebo, and why it matters less than you think
• How this study is being used in rescheduling efforts
• How vested interests fuel anti-cannabis research

Summary

In this episode, Bryan Fields and Kellan Finney engage with Ryan Castle, Research Director at Whole Health Oncology Institute, to explore the evolving landscape of medical cannabis research. Ryan shares his journey from skepticism to advocacy, detailing the extensive meta-analysis he conducted on the efficacy of cannabis in treating various symptoms and conditions, particularly in oncology. The conversation delves into the challenges of measuring effectiveness, the importance of patient-reported outcomes, and the need for a shift in medical perspectives towards cannabis as a legitimate treatment option. Ryan emphasizes the potential impact of policy changes and the importance of transparency in research, while also discussing the Cancer Playbook initiative aimed at empowering patients with data-driven insights.


Takeaways

Ryan Castle initially set out to prove that cannabis doesn't work.
His extensive research revealed that cannabis is effective for a wide range of conditions.
The meta-analysis included over 10,000 studies and 800,000 data points.
Cannabis showed efficacy not just for symptoms but also for cancer treatment.
Patient-reported outcomes are crucial for understanding cannabis effectiveness.

There is a significant need for a shift in medical perspectives on cannabis.
Transparency in research is essential for building trust in findings.
The health impact assessment could reveal the broader benefits of cannabis.

title: Hard Truths for MSOs — What Canada’s LPs Already Learned ft. Mitchell Osak

The bigger problem? Too many companies are chasing the wrong metrics and ignoring the lessons other industries already learned.

This week we sit down with Mitchell Osak — a veteran strategist across pharma, CPG, financial services, and cannabis — to unpack the hard truths and strategy lessons MSOs can’t afford to miss.

In this episode we cover:
• The wrong metrics driving cannabis off course — and which ones Mitch would track instead
• Why TAM slides are the biggest lie in cannabis strategy
•  Which playbooks cannabis should borrow from pharma, wine, and tech

title: THC Is an Ingredient: How Pharma, MSOs & Hemp Converge After Schedule III ft. Zach Edge
description:

Cannabinoids will be treated like standardized inputs across pharma, licensed cannabis, and hemp—and the future winners are hedging until there’s clarity.

Near term, expect Schedule III to unlock e-pharmacy distribution and centralized GMP manufacturing, while tobacco pushes device rules, alcohol shapes low-dose beverage norms, and hemp keeps expanding.

This chaotic industry is about to get even crazier.

This week we sit down with Zach Edge to discuss:

title: This Mistake Is Killing Your Plants — Dr. Greenhouse (Nadia Sabeh)
description:
What if keeping the room a little too dry is killing your plants?

Humidity—and the HVAC that controls it—drives plant health, but air isn’t uniform across the room. The fix isn’t more AC; it’s dialing VPD so humidity, lights, airflow, and irrigation work together. Get it wrong and you lose yield and fail tests; get it right and buds stay sticky, healthy, and consistent.

This week we sit down with Dr. Greenhouse (aka Nadia Sabeh) to discuss:

• Dry ≠ safe: why extra-dry rooms can actually spread powdery mildew
• Measure where it matters: a simple toolkit and method at the canopy
• Design for airflow: room shapes and layouts that keep climate even

The conversation delves into root cause analysis, the significance of understanding plant needs, and the necessity of proper data collection to improve cultivation practices. title: Hemp vs. THC: The Cannabis Drink Showdown
description:
Hemp beverages have exploded over the last 24 months, and they are likely the tip of the spear for broader cannabis reform, helping to normalize cannabis through a familiar form factor.

The opportunity to produce hemp-based products in a single facility and distribute them across state lines offers benefits throughout the supply chain, providing consumers with more cost-effective products-much like how global giants like Coca-Cola operate. However, the rules governing this are still very grey.

In contrast, regulated markets require brands like Keef to establish individual operations in each state, leading to massive capital expenditures and challenging returns, especially when confined to a single state's population. Now, Keef sometimes finds itself competing with others-or even itself-as those who can distribute more broadly enjoy better unit economics without the burden of regulatory headaches and infrastructure costs.

Balancing these two models-considering the investments, the state of the market, and the opportunities at hand-is far from simple. Especially when you consider that Keef has been pioneering cannabis beverages for the past 14 years.

This week, we sit down with Erik Knutson to discuss:

• Building a beverage brand in 2010
• The differences between the regulated cannabis market and the hemp-derived market
• Key manufacturing and strategy decisions
• And much more

Eric shares the story of how Keef Brands was founded, starting with their initial focus on cannabis-infused beverages and the challenges they faced in developing the manufacturing process.

Eric discusses Keef Brands' expansion efforts, the challenges of licensing their brand in different states, and the importance of vetting partnerships.

About Sundie Seefried:

Safe Harbor Financial is the brainchild of Sundie Seefried. A 35-year veteran of the credit union industry, in 2014, she saw that CRBs needed financial services and that Colorado communities would be safer if the new industry had access to banking solutions.

A 39-year credit union industry veteran, Seefried was the former CEO of Partner Colorado Credit Union (PCCU). Established in 2015 by PCCU, Safe Harbor was formed to provide an unmet need – compliant banking and financial services to the rapidly growing U.S. cannabis industry. Seefried designed a full scope Cannabis Banking Program for PCCU known as the Safe Harbor program, which has withstood the scrutiny of 16 federal and state exams to date. Now in its 8th year, Safe Harbor has grown to nearly 600 accounts spanning 20 states, and processed over $12 billion in cannabis-related transactions.

Seefried regularly provides cannabis banking education and expertise to legislators, regulators, attorneys generals, state officials, and financial institutions. She is on a mission to normalize banking for the cannabis industry, while assisting law enforcement and federal agencies to be more effective at combating illicit activities and protecting the financial system.

To share her knowledge, Seefried authored the book 'Navigating Safe Harbor – Cannabis Banking in Uncertain Times' in 2016, as well as contributed a chapter on cannabis banking in the university textbook 'The Politics of Marijuana: A New Paradigm' by Timothy McGettigan.

title: From One of the Nation's First Licensed Medical Operators to Kingpin Statute: Luke Scarmazzo's Story
description:
Imagine this. You operate a state-licensed business. You pay your taxes and follow ALL the rules and regulations as defined.

You hear a knock at your home door on your daughter's birthday. U.S. federal Agents are there to charge you with the Kingpin Statute or the same law designed to target El Chapo and other cartel leaders.

Not only have you never been convicted of a crime, but you have also followed all the rules California enacted when they passed the Compassionate Use Act in 1996 

Certainly, a jury of your peers who voted for this law almost a decade earlier would be an arbitrator of truth and fair would recognize you’re not a drug kingpin, let alone a criminal. This is the United States of America. 

This week we sit down with Luke Scarmazzo, One of the first licensed medical dispensaries in the United States, who shares his compelling story.

We discuss: 

● 2004 California Cannabis Industry
● Scarmazzo vs. United States of America
● Emotional rollercoaster

● And so much more

About Luke Scarmazzo

In 2006, Luke Scarmazzo was running a state-legal medical cannabis dispensary in Modesto, California, when he was arrested by U.S. federal agents following a DEA raid of the business. Scarmazzo was prosecuted in federal court and received a 22-year jail sentence. He and his family have turned to The Weldon Project for support.

Though Scarmazzo’s dispensary was legal through California’s Proposition 215 – which legalized medical cultivation, sales, and consumption in the state – he and his business partner were charged under the Continuing Criminal Enterprise Statute. The CCE Statute, also known as the Kingpin Statute, is a federal law designed to target large-scale drug traffickers and cartels who are responsible for long-term and elaborate drug conspiracies. It carries a mandatory minimum jail sentence of 20 years.

In 2017, after serving nearly a decade in jail, Scarmazzo petitioned the Obama administration for commutation. His business partner, Ricardo Montes, received clemency, but Luke’s request was denied. In 2020, advocates with the nonprofit The Weldon Project included Luke's name on a list of 25 marijuana offenders sent to the Trump White House as part of a clemency campaign supported by Republicans, Democrats, law enforcement and various celebrities. Although President Trump granted nine of the requested pardons, Luke’s request was not granted.
